items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Charlie Shavers had a great little group there.

ctx.x: his then-band there on the bandstand and the people standing around. Nat is in that photograph, but he’s misidentified. The Central Plaza was a memorable – there was a lot of wonderful music being played there. Fletcher Henderson came one night and played with a small group, reconstructed alumni. Jonah Jones was on trumpet. He had not yet made it with Muted Jazz. He was very little known. Gene Sedric. I forget who was on drums. Fletcher, he was already in the final stages of his life, but he was still a very…

on drums, whom I knew. That’s how I first met Roy. Charlie Shavers had a great little group there. That was when [Hot] Lips [Page] sat in with Charlie. I remember they played Royal Garden Blues. Lips hit a high note and passed out. He just slid down. He was leaning against a wall at the bandstand, and he just slid down. He revived very quickly, but everybody was concerned about him. Later on, he was sitting at the bar recovering. Big Sid Catlett was in the house. I remember, because I was right next to them. Sid…
Before we get into the Army, I think you should recount your first meeting with Louis Armstrong.

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: on the floor sitting at his feet was Charlie Shavers, the great trumpet player and a terrific — what a great guy Charlie was.

ctx.x: Well this was not too terribly long after I came to New York and I had met this little underground trumpet player named Matt Lorber, nickname was “Face”; he knew everybody and everybody knew him, and also met a very hip young lady who was the first to take me to the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and that actually turned out to be a night when Dizzy’s big band was appearing there with Chano Pozo, so I got to see that, which was tremendous. The Apollo was — one thing of course — the Apollo was frequented to some extent…

going, but it wasn’t what it used to be. But there were little clubs and there was this wonderful trumpet player and singer named Hot Lips Page. Lips was my friend, Nat was a kind of protégé of Lips’. Lips was from Texas and he didn’t call him “Face” but he called him “Shorty” which was pronounced “Shouty” — that was his Texas accent. And going to Harlem, Lips lived there, was a wonderful experience. There were after hours places, and the after hours places could be somebody’s apartment where there was an old…
